references.text: Elisha followed Elijah after the call, but first asked to say goodbye to his father and mother. This is the Old Testament background for the scene in Luke 9:61, where a person wants to follow Jesus but first wishes to say farewell to those at home.
The preceding verses in the same pericope deal with others who want to follow Jesus but set conditions or face radical demands. Verse 61 is the third in this series of discipleship conversations.

Jesus' answer to the request in verse 61: 'No one who puts their hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.' This shows that Jesus' call to discipleship is more radical than Elijah's call to Elisha.
Jesus speaks about carrying his cross and the conditions for being his disciple. Following Jesus requires putting him before everything else, including family ties—the same theme as in 9:61.
A parallel in Matthew where a disciple asks to be allowed to bury his father first, and Jesus responds with a radical call to discipleship without delay.
'The one who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.' Jesus emphasizes that discipleship requires placing him above family relationships, as in Luke 9:61.

Paul speaks about forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead—not looking back but pressing toward the goal. This principle of wholeheartedness in discipleship reflects Jesus' point in Luke 9:61-62.

People of faith did not look back to the land they had left, but longed for a better homeland. Their wholehearted faith without looking back illustrates what Jesus requires of his followers in Luke 9:61.
